cards.explanation: The answer is that Sheba calls the men of Israel to walk away from David. Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, shouts, "Every man to his tent, O Israel!" (2 Samuel 20:1). It's the old "I'm out, everybody grab your coats" move. One shout, and he's asking a whole crowd to head for the door.

The group that deserts David is all the men of Israel. The text says, "…all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri." (2 Samuel 20:2) I've been left in a drawer before, friends, and I'm telling you, that kind of leaving stings. The men of Judah stayed by their king, but Israel's men left him for Sheba.

The answer is True, friends, and the text says it plainly. "But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem." (2 Samuel 20:2) While the men of Israel go after Sheba, Judah stays right with David. That's a long way to stay beside him.

The word is widows. David puts the ten concubines in a house under guard and provides for them, and they live as widows until the day they die (2 Samuel 20:3). I think this is one of the heavy parts of the chapter. It's hard to read, and it's okay to sit with that for a second.

The answer is three days. David says, "Summon the men of Judah to come to me within three days, and be here yourself." (2 Samuel 20:4). Amasa, the man David told to gather Judah, gets a short, clear deadline. Three days is plenty to set a few alarms.

The answer is False. Amasa goes to summon Judah, but he takes longer than the time allotted him (2 Samuel 20:5). We've all been the one saying "almost there" while the clock keeps going. I'll be honest, friends, I've done that with a batch or two myself.

The answer is fortified cities. David tells Abishai, Joab's brother, to pursue Sheba "…or he will find fortified cities and elude us." (2 Samuel 20:6). Walled cities are hard to get into. So David wants Sheba caught before he can get behind one.

The answer is True, and that's what makes it so chilling. Joab, who was over David's army (2 Samuel 20:23), asks Amasa, "Are you well, my brother?" and takes him by the beard to kiss him (2 Samuel 20:9). All that while the dagger is already out of its sheath (2 Samuel 20:8). It sounds friendly, and that's the danger of it.

The answer is that Joab kills Amasa with the dagger. Joab stabs Amasa in the stomach, and he doesn't need to strike again, for Amasa is dead (2 Samuel 20:10). I think this is one of the hardest parts of the chapter. It's heavy, and it's okay that it feels that way.

The word is stop. The text says the man "…saw that all the troops were stopping there…" while Amasa lay in the middle of the road (2 Samuel 20:12). A whole army is stopping right there. Then the young man drags the body off the road into a field and throws a garment over it.

The answer is True. The young man drags the body into a field and throws a garment over it, and "As soon as Amasa’s body was removed from the road, all the men went on with Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri." (2 Samuel 20:12-13). The road is clear and the chase is back on. Nobody is standing around anymore.
The city is Abel-beth-maacah. Joab's troops besiege Sheba there (2 Samuel 20:15). Sheba had passed through all the tribes of Israel to get there (2 Samuel 20:14). That's where the chase ends.

The answer is True. The troops build a siege ramp against the outer rampart, and all of them are "…battering the wall to topple it…" (2 Samuel 20:15). That's an army that came to work. It's a lot of hammering on one city wall.

The word is woman. A wise woman calls out from the city, "Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him." (2 Samuel 20:16). The text never gives her name. All it says is that she's wise, and her words end up settling the whole matter.

She asks Joab why he would swallow up the LORD's inheritance, and that's a sharp question. She asks, "Why would you swallow up the LORD’s inheritance?" (2 Samuel 20:19). She says she's among the peaceable and faithful in Israel, and that her city is "…a mother in Israel." She called out from the city to ask it (2 Samuel 20:16).

Joab wants Sheba handed over to him. Joab says Sheba son of Bichri has lifted up his hand against the king, and tells the woman, "Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city." (2 Samuel 20:21). He wants one man, not the whole city. That's a pretty short list of demands.

The answer is False. She tells Joab, "…his head will be thrown to you over the wall." (2 Samuel 20:21). I think this is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't soften it. She promises his head, not a man handed over alive.

Joab's men each go to their own home. Joab blows the ram's horn, and his men disperse from the city, "…each to his own home." (2 Samuel 20:22). The same kind of horn that started the rebellion now ends the siege. The army goes home.

The answer is True. The text says, "And Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem." (2 Samuel 20:22). The chase that began with one horn ends with Joab back with David. This is the last stretch of Absalom's whole story.
